nameStory: The Black Swallowtail gets its name from its predominantly black wings adorned with the characteristic 'tail' extensions that all swallowtail butterflies share. These tail-like projections on the hindwings resemble the deeply forked tail of a swallow in flight. The species is also called the 'parsnip swallowtail' because its caterpillars love to munch on plants in the carrot family, including parsley, dill, and wild parsnips.
description: The Black Swallowtail is a large, striking butterfly with predominantly black wings decorated with rows of yellow spots and brilliant blue scaling. Males tend to have more prominent yellow markings, while females show more subdued coloring with blue highlights. These butterflies have a wingspan of about 3-4 inches and are strong, graceful fliers that seem to dance through gardens and meadows. The distinctive tail projections on their hindwings make them unmistakable as members of the swallowtail family.

idTips.label: Wing Pattern
idTips.description: Look for the distinctive double row of yellow spots running parallel along the wing edges, creating a polka-dot border effect against the velvety black background

idTips.label: Hindwing Tails
idTips.description: Each hindwing has a prominent tail-like extension with a bright orange eyespot ringed in black - these tails flutter distinctively in flight

idTips.label: Blue Scaling
idTips.description: The hindwings shimmer with iridescent blue scales that catch the light, especially prominent in females and more subdued in males

idTips.label: Flight Style
idTips.description: Watch for their characteristic slow, sailing flight pattern with deep wingbeats - they seem to float and glide rather than flutter frantically

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: These are substantial butterflies that feel surprisingly sturdy if handled gently - much larger and more robust than common garden butterflies like cabbage whites

idTips.label: Caterpillar Form
idTips.description: The 'parsley worm' caterpillars are plump, green with black bands and yellow spots, and will pop out bright orange 'horns' when disturbed - they smell strongly of carrot when touched

habitat: Black Swallowtails thrive in open, sunny areas including gardens, fields, meadows, and roadsides where their host plants grow abundantly. Look for them especially in areas with wild carrot, parsley, dill, fennel, and other plants in the carrot family. They're equally at home in suburban gardens and rural farmland, from sea level to moderate elevations throughout New England.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late April and May, with males typically appearing first to establish territories. This is when you'll see the most intense courtship activity.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs from June through August when multiple generations overlap. Look for both adults nectaring on flowers and distinctive striped caterpillars munching on garden herbs.
seasonality.fall: The final generation appears in September and early October, with some individuals migrating south while others overwinter as pupae. Late-season adults often seem larger and more vibrant.
seasonality.winter: Black Swallowtails overwinter as brown, stick-like pupae attached to plant stems or structures. No adult activity occurs during New England's cold months.

funFact: When Black Swallowtail caterpillars feel threatened, they instantly pop out a pair of bright orange, horn-like organs called osmeterium from behind their heads while releasing a smell that's been described as a mix of pineapple and rotten socks - this startling transformation can make even seasoned gardeners jump!
confusionNotes: Black Swallowtails are most often confused with Spicebush Swallowtails, but remember 'spots vs. smudges' - Black Swallowtails have neat rows of distinct yellow spots while Spicebush Swallowtails have more diffuse, cloudy light markings that look like someone smudged chalk on their wings.
contextualKnowledge: This butterfly is named after Polyxena from Greek mythology, the youngest daughter of King Priam of Troy, though the connection between the tragic princess and this garden visitor remains a mystery of scientific naming. Many gardeners unknowingly host these butterflies by growing culinary herbs like parsley and dill, making them one of the few butterflies that directly benefits from herb gardening.
compareHints: Among New England's swallowtails, Black Swallowtails are the most 'polka-dotted' with their precise yellow spots, while Eastern Tiger Swallowtails are predominantly yellow with black stripes, and Spicebush Swallowtails have greenish-blue highlights with blurry pale markings. Black Swallowtails also tend to fly lower and more slowly than the powerful, high-soaring Tiger Swallowtails.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's swallowtails, spicebush swallowtails are the darkest and most consistently black, lacking the yellow stripes of tiger swallowtails or the yellow spot-bands of black swallowtails.
Among New England's swallowtails, Eastern Tiger Swallowtails are the largest and most boldly striped when yellow.

Unlike the Black Swallowtail which is much smaller and primarily black with blue markings, or the Spicebush Swallowtail which has more blue-green iridescence, the Canadian Tiger Swallowtail maintains its yellow and black tiger pattern in both sexes.
Compared to the Eastern Tiger Swallowtail, the midsummer species has a distinct later flight period and is often slightly smaller with more vivid coloration.
